title: Hermes Agent Consultant · Advanced: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: What is the core reason for forming a legal entity rather than contracting as an individual?
options: To reduce the tax the practice pays on consulting income.
To separate the practice's obligations from the person's, so a liability does not reach personal assets.
To make invoicing simpler for enterprise clients.
To allow the practice to hire contractors without a written agreement.
questions.explanation: An entity separates the practice's obligations from the person's, so a claim against the company does not reach personal assets.

questions.question: Which three tools bound what each agent in a fleet is allowed to do?
options: Isolation, permission, and audit.
Throughput, latency, and cost.
Hiring, onboarding, and review.
Demand, competence, and repeatability.
questions.explanation: Isolation confines each agent's reach, least-privilege permission limits the actions it may attempt, and audit keeps a trace so accountability survives at scale.

questions.question: What does the practice require of the ownership of its functions?
options: Every function has a named owner, so when a person leaves their functions are already named and can be reassigned.
The principal should own every function until the practice can afford a dedicated operator.
Ownership can stay implicit as long as the team is small and communicates well.
Only the reference architectures and internal tooling need named owners.
questions.explanation: Named ownership means a departure surfaces no hidden dependency, since each function is already assigned to someone.

questions.question: What is the real measure that a consulting practice has scaled?
options: Growing headcount until the team can carry more concurrent client engagements.
How much the practice's annual revenue has grown over the prior year.
Whether deliverables still meet the bar when the principal is unavailable.
How many named clients the practice has signed across all its segments.
questions.explanation: Scaling is defined by how much work the practice can deliver without the principal's judgment in the path, not by headcount or revenue.

questions.question: What sets the throughput of a delivery system?
options: The total number of people and agents it has.
The binding constraint, the slowest stage everything else queues behind.
The average utilization of the delivery team.
The size of the sales pipeline feeding it.
questions.explanation: Throughput is capped by the constraint, so adding capacity anywhere below it raises utilization without adding output, and the earliest honest signal is a growing queue in front of the constraint.

questions.question: What does the onboarding exit gate require before a new hire is finished?
options: Comfort with the team and familiarity with the tools.
The ability to run a defined engagement arc to standard, behind review gates, without the principal touching a deliverable.
Completion of a fixed reading list and a written exam.
A signed acknowledgment that the method has been read.
questions.explanation: Onboarding ends with a measurable gate, not a feeling: the hire can run the engagement arc to the same standard any engagement must meet, with the principal only reading health reports.

questions.question: Where is most scope creep actually prevented?
options: In scoping and the proposal, by naming every deliverable, assumption, and exclusion.
In change control, once the engagement is underway and requests arrive.
In the contract, by reserving the right to re-price new requests.
In delivery, by absorbing small requests so the client stays happy.
questions.explanation: A vague boundary at scoping is what invites later creep, so the proposal is where the tight scope and its exclusions are set.

questions.question: What should a principal actually hire for?
options: Prior experience with the exact tooling and a strong individual track record.
The ability to fill the role the principal used to hold personally.
A slot in the delivery method: faithfulness to it plus judgment where it does not cover.
Willingness to work long hours and take on every kind of task.
questions.explanation: The role is a slot in a captured method, so the two things to evaluate are whether the person runs the playbook as built and whether they flag the moments it does not cover instead of improvising past them.

questions.question: A client asks who will actually do the work. Which answer marks a principal rather than a consultant who employs staff?
options: I will, and I will stay on it personally until it is done.
The practice will: the method, the playbook, and the staffed team carry it.
A contractor will, and I will check in at the end.
Whoever is free, and I will supervise every step closely.
questions.explanation: A principal sells capacity and points at the delivery system, so the result does not depend on any one person's hands being on the work.

questions.question: What does design authority own that governance does not?
options: The state each agent can touch and the tools it may call.
The standard of quality and the power to reject work that fails it.
The schedule of which engagements run in which period.
The budget each engagement is allowed to spend.
questions.explanation: Governance bounds each agent's reach, while authority sets what counts as good and must be exercised continuously by a role with the standing to say no.

questions.question: What structure makes a value-based deal survivable?
options: A floor that covers delivery cost and baseline margin, plus a share of measured value above the baseline.
A pure contingency paid only if the outcome actually lands.
A fixed price reverse-engineered from estimated hours and a rate.
An hourly rate with a bonus paid at the client's discretion.
questions.explanation: Without a floor, a value-based fee makes the practice carry cost and outcome risk with nothing underneath, so the base fee keeps it solvent on the work and the share is the upside.

questions.question: A practice shows strong contribution on every unit but a negative practice margin. What does that reveal?
options: That the flagship offer is underpriced relative to the value it delivers.
That the fixed-cost base is too heavy for the volume of units sold.
That the delivery cost of each unit is higher than the market rate.
That the practice's runway must be longer than twelve months to be safe.
questions.explanation: Unit contribution pays the fixed base; when contribution is healthy but practice margin is negative, the fixed base is too large for the volume of units sold.

questions.question: What does choosing among hourly, productized, and value-based pricing actually decide?
options: How sophisticated the practice appears to prospective clients.
Which risks the practice is willing to own and can price.
The maximum hourly rate the practice can quote.
The number of offers the catalog is allowed to carry.
questions.explanation: Each model is an allocation of risk: hourly leaves delivery risk with the client, productized moves it to the practice, and value-based shares outcome risk, so the real question is which risks you can price.

questions.question: How do the estimate and the price relate to each other?
options: The price is the estimate plus a standard markup the practice chooses.
The estimate is internal effort against the practice's method, while the price is the value the market will bear.
The estimate should equal the price so the delivery team is protected.
The price is the estimate discounted by whatever the buyer's budget allows.
questions.explanation: The estimate answers an internal effort question, while the price is a separate judgment about what the work is worth to the buyer.

questions.question: A buyer challenges the price and says other vendors quoted less. What is the sound response?
options: Offer a discount to keep the deal alive, since a lost deal costs more than a thinner margin.
Explain that the other vendors are not credible and ask the buyer to disregard them.
Reduce the scope silently to fit the lower price without telling the buyer.
Return to the value: restate what changes, what it is worth, and what it costs the buyer not to act.
questions.explanation: A price challenge usually means the buyer does not yet see the value; discounting teaches that the price was arbitrary, while returning to value answers the real question.

questions.question: Which set names the kinds of intellectual property a healthy practice builds?
options: Method, templates, reference architecture, internal tooling, and accumulated findings.
Proposals, invoices, contracts, time sheets, and expense reports.
Demand, competence, repeatability, margin, and utilization.
Discovery, build, review, handover, and support.
questions.explanation: These five are the reusable assets underneath an offer: the way work is done, the starting points for deliverables, the canonical design, the automating tooling, and the record of what worked.

questions.question: Why is excellent delivery not enough on its own to bring work in the door?
options: Because buyers judge the promise of delivery before they can evaluate it.
Because strong delivery tends to make a team complacent about its own quality.
Because referrals stop arriving once a practice leaves hourly billing behind.
Because buyers insist on evaluating delivery before agreeing to any first call.
questions.explanation: A buyer purchases the promise of delivery as it is represented in positioning, offer, and proof, so excellent work stays invisible without a plan to present it.

questions.question: A practice is deciding whether to pursue a certification. What is the sound approach?
options: Pursue every major certification so the practice can answer any procurement question.
Skip certification entirely and rely on internal records as evidence.
Build the system because it improves the work, then certify only when a real buyer gates on it.
Buy the certificate first, then let the system catch up.
questions.explanation: Certification is worth buying only where a buyer actually requires it; the system itself should be built to improve the work, not to win a badge.

questions.question: Why is the unit of analysis for portfolio management the account rather than a single engagement?
options: Because accounts are billed monthly while engagements are billed on milestones.
Because the levers cross engagement boundaries, so the relationship needs an owner accountable beyond the work in flight.
Because clients insist on one point of contact for commercial questions.
Because engagement-level data is not available in the delivery system.
questions.explanation: The expansion, renewal, and churn levers act on the whole relationship, so the unit of analysis is the account rather than one engagement.

questions.question: Why should a status cadence run on a fixed schedule even when there is no news to report?
options: Because clients require a report every period regardless of its content.
Because an activity log reassures the committee that the team is busy.
Because a report that always arrives and tells the truth makes bad news believed when it appears.
Because the report is the only record that makes a decision auditable.
questions.explanation: A cadence that runs on schedule regardless of the news builds trust, so a flagged problem is taken seriously instead of read as a routine alarm.

questions.question: In a knowledge practice, what does codification accomplish?
options: It raises the hourly rate the practice can charge its clients.
It keeps the method inside the principal's head for tighter control.
It turns the judgment used to do the work into a repeatable system others can run.
It removes the need for judgment from every part of the work.
questions.explanation: Codification captures the small decisions an experienced person makes automatically so a competent executor can run them without the original expert in the room; judgment is reserved for the moments that truly need it.

questions.question: Why must the separation of the author from the reviewer come before the other separations?
options: Because clients expect a written review process before they sign any work.
Because a second seller cannot be brought on until the pricing model is fully built.
Because without a review gate, more deliverers only add unsupervised output.
Because the principal must stop billing hours before any other capacity can be added.
questions.explanation: A review gate against a written standard is what makes good work repeatable; without it, more deliverers multiply unsupervised output rather than real capacity.

questions.question: As a practice grows from one engagement to many, how does the principal's focus shift?
options: From a single project's outcome to the health of the whole portfolio.
From the quality of each deliverable to the size of the team.
From delivery risk to the marketing of new service lines.
From billable hours to the number of clients on the roster.
questions.explanation: A portfolio is made or broken by the pattern across engagements, such as utilization, margin, and concentrated risk, not by any single project.

questions.question: A principal must choose between a quarter that personally bills a large engagement and a quarter spent building a new lead and a new service line. How should the two be compared?
options: On revenue, because the personally billed work funds later development.
On the principal's own utilization, because that measures the scarce resource.
On client satisfaction, because a strong reputation drives future referrals.
On which option increases the work the firm can carry without the principal.
questions.explanation: The right comparison is which option moves the firm further toward running without the founder, since revenue can grow while the practice stays dependent on one person.

questions.question: Which orchestration pattern fits work that splits into many independent pieces and then recombines?
options: Orchestrator and worker, which routes every piece through one coordinator.
A pipeline, which moves work through a fixed sequence of stages.
Fan-out and merge, which splits one trigger into parallel workers and combines the results.
A single long-running agent that handles every stage on its own.
questions.explanation: Fan-out and merge is the pattern for embarrassingly parallel work; its trade-off is that the merge must combine many outputs without losing consistency.

questions.question: Why is 100 percent utilization a warning rather than a win?
options: It shows the practice is finally working at full efficiency.
It means the utilization denominator was defined too strictly.
It leaves no slack to absorb the unexpected, so every new demand becomes a queue.
It signals the practice has too many staff for its demand.
questions.explanation: Slack is the buffer that lets the system respond, and when nothing is free, an emergency, a failed review, or a new opportunity has nowhere to go, so the cost shows up later as rework and burnout.

questions.question: A go-to-market plan is built from decisions, not aspirations. What makes a section a decision?
options: It names the marketing software the practice will run the plan on.
It commits to a choice that closes off a real alternative.
It sets a quarterly revenue target the whole team is accountable to.
It selects the single competitor the practice will position against.
questions.explanation: Every part of the plan is a commitment that closes off alternatives, which is what lets someone other than the author execute it.

questions.question: What is the strategic test for whether an expansion genuinely improves the portfolio?
options: Reuse: whether the next engagement can lean on captured skills and method, so marginal cost falls.
Whether the account will pay a higher rate for the second engagement than the first.
Whether the expansion keeps the delivery team at full utilization.
Whether the expansion is larger in revenue than the engagement it follows.
questions.explanation: An expansion compounds only when it reuses existing capability, lowering marginal cost instead of pulling the team into a new domain.

questions.question: Why model a practice's finances at the unit level instead of in annual totals?
options: Because annual totals hide the fixed costs that unit modeling exposes.
Because lenders require unit economics before they will extend credit.
Because annual profit is too volatile and unpredictable to model at all.
Because the unit is where price, cost, and volume can be acted on.
questions.explanation: Unit-level numbers expose the price, cost, and volume levers a principal can actually act on; aggregate totals collapse them together.

questions.question: Two practices show the same healthy per-unit contribution but different runway. What does the runway difference determine?
options: Which one can afford to spend a quarter on non-delivery work.
Which one has the higher contribution per unit on its offers.
Which one has the lower variable delivery cost per unit.
Which one can raise prices without losing any existing clients.
questions.explanation: Runway is the budget that makes an investment available; a thin runway forces survival decisions while a long one lets the firm absorb a quarter without revenue.

questions.question: Why is retention the single biggest lever on a recurring revenue business?
options: Because a retained dollar keeps paying, while a new one must be won.
Because retained clients always agree to pay a higher monthly fee.
Because retention removes all variable delivery cost from an account.
Because high retention lets a practice stop measuring its margins.
questions.explanation: A retained client keeps paying at a lower retention cost, so improving retention compounds, while each new client must be won again from zero.

questions.question: What distinguishes a true client partnership from a vendor relationship?
options: The client renews the contract without renegotiating its terms each cycle.
The client reports strong satisfaction in an annual relationship review.
The client pays a recurring fee each month rather than per project.
The client raises problems early and consults before they become urgent.
questions.explanation: Satisfaction and renewal can both happen without commitment; a partner is given early access to problems and roadmap, the raw material that can only be earned.

questions.question: Which packaging mistake destroys the margin the exercise was meant to protect?
options: Writing an explicit scope boundary into the offer.
Setting the price from the outcome the client gains.
Cutting the offer into a cheap, thin product and competing on price.
Building delivery machinery once and reusing it across sales.
questions.explanation: Productizing is not commoditizing: if an offer is stripped down and sold cheaply, the price stops tracking the value delivered and the practice ends up with worse economics than a solo consultant.

questions.question: Why is separating the practice's money from the founder's personal money the first financial act?
options: Because it is required before the practice can file a tax return.
Because mixing the two makes the founder personally liable for business debts.
Because a practice whose revenue and cost land in one set of books can compute what it costs to deliver, so it can price.
Because clients will not contract with a practice that pays personal expenses.
questions.explanation: Separate books are what make revenue and cost comparable, which is the only way to know what it costs to deliver and how to price.

questions.question: When is the right moment to escalate a risk on a large engagement?
options: Wait until the next committee sitting so the escalation lands in the right forum.
Escalate only after the delivery lead has exhausted every internal option.
Escalate once the cost of the risk is large enough to justify the client's attention.
Escalate the moment the risk is visible and still actionable, since not escalating is the real failure.
questions.explanation: Escalating early costs a short conversation while waiting costs rework and lost trust, so the first visible, actionable moment is the right one.

questions.question: A steering committee on a large engagement keeps drifting into a recap of completed work instead of making decisions. What does a written charter prevent?
options: It lists the decisions that belong to the committee, so the group decides rather than narrates.
It lists the meeting dates and the attendees, so authority follows the calendar.
It lists the escalation thresholds, so the committee handles only tripped risks.
It lists the delivery plan, so the committee exists mainly to approve it.
questions.explanation: A charter names the decisions the committee owns; without one the group defaults to narration and slowly stops deciding anything.

questions.question: What tells a principal that a control on the risk register is actually handling a risk rather than being cosmetic?
options: The risk is named on the register and reviewed on a schedule.
The risk has a written appetite statement signed by the principal.
The risk appears in the client contract and in its data terms.
The gap between the inherent exposure and the residual exposure after the control runs.
questions.explanation: The value of a control is the reduction it produces, so the gap between inherent and residual exposure is what shows it is doing real work.

questions.question: Why must a design reviewer be independent of the builder?
options: Because nobody reliably rejects their own work, so self-approval is a formality.
Because independent reviewers are cheaper to staff than builders.
Because independent reviewers work faster than the builder does.
Because the builder is usually unavailable when review is due.
questions.explanation: A review can only enforce the standard if it can say no, and the person closest to the work is biased toward it, so the approval must sit with a role that exists to be skeptical.

questions.question: What test separates a real go-to-market plan from an aspiration?
options: Whether an advisor outside the practice has approved the document.
Whether every section names a revenue target and a deadline for it.
Whether the document lists both inbound and outbound marketing motions.
Whether a competent stranger could run the document for a quarter.
questions.explanation: A plan is executable by someone other than its author; a section a competent stranger cannot run is a resolution, not a decision.

questions.question: A recurring account's invoice stays flat while the cost of delivering it creeps up. Which risk does that describe?
options: Concentration risk from a single anchor client dominating the base.
The vendor trap, where a partnership quietly decays into a low-touch subscription.
Margin drift, where a deliverable's margin erodes while the invoice holds.
Value drift, where a fee tied to an outcome stops matching the result.
questions.explanation: Margin drift is silent because the invoice holds steady while rising delivery cost erodes the margin, which is why accounts are measured on a margin cadence.

questions.question: What are the three clauses of a well-formed unit of work?
options: The owner, the budget, and the deadline.
The goal, the boundary, and the definition of done.
The input, the output, and the reviewer.
The scope, the price, and the duration.
questions.explanation: With a goal, a boundary that keeps agents from overlapping, and an explicit definition of done, any competent executor can pick up the work, so it is not tied to one agent and can be handed off mid-flight.

questions.question: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: Control applies to software deliverables and assurance applies to client relationships.
Control inspects an output and decides whether it passes, while assurance shapes the process so defects do not arise.
Control is documented and assurance is informal.
Control is done by the author and assurance by an external auditor.
questions.explanation: Control is inspection at the point of delivery, while assurance designs the process so the defect is never created, which is cheaper.

questions.question: What capture discipline turns delivered work into an asset?
options: Writing an annual summary of the practice's strengths.
Reusing client-specific material across engagements to save effort.
Recording the method and know-how while the work happens, in a form others can load and run.
Keeping the method in the heads of the people who did the work.
questions.explanation: Doing good work is not the same as building IP; the work is consumed unless the method and know-how are captured deliberately and made loadable, or they leak away and the practice stays small.

questions.question: What is the failure mode of accumulated machinery that is never reviewed?
options: It outlives its accuracy, so a stale pattern is trusted and followed with confidence.
It grows faster than the practice can document it.
It becomes too specific to the clients it was built for.
It discourages the team from solving new problems from first principles.
questions.explanation: A stale pattern is worse than no pattern because it is trusted, so each asset needs an owner and a review cadence.

questions.question: A high-potential operator two years from principal is already performing well. Which relationship do they actually need?
options: More management, because objectives and role performance are still unproven.
Coaching on how to work faster within the current role.
Mentoring on judgment and sponsorship into the room where the client relationship and the numbers live.
All four relationships at once, so nothing is missed.
questions.explanation: A high performer needs the relationships that expand capability: mentoring on judgment and sponsorship into rooms where development can happen.

questions.question: A practice runs every engagement on one shared agent and one shared memory store. What control turns cross-client bleed into a property of the system?
options: Have operators delete any client material they notice in the shared store.
Keep a written policy that client contexts must never be mixed.
Run each engagement in its own isolated profile with its own memory and state, so separation is structural.
Ask the model provider to guarantee that client data stays separate.
questions.explanation: Isolation through separate profiles turns a discipline that depends on memory into a verifiable property of the system.

questions.question: What distinguishes senior delivery talent from a mid-level operator?
options: The ability to author the standard: write the criteria, place the gate, review others, and own the estimate.
More years of experience across a wider range of clients.
A higher utilization rate on client-billable work.
The habit of escalating fewer problems over time.
questions.explanation: The step up is owning the framework, authoring the standard and review, not just performing well inside it.

questions.question: What makes an offer buyable in a way a service line is not?
options: An offer names a domain of capability the practice is good at.
An offer is a specific, priced, scoped deliverable a client can accept or reject.
An offer describes what the practice could do if it were engaged.
An offer lists the skills the practice has assembled over time.
questions.explanation: A service line is a category no client can transact on; an offer pins down the deliverable, outcome, price, and entry criteria so it becomes something a client can say yes to.

questions.question: How does intellectual property behave differently from an offer?
options: An offer is priced, while IP is given away with each engagement.
An offer is consumed when sold, while IP is an asset that improves as it is used.
An offer is owned by the client, while IP is owned by the practice.
An offer compounds over time, while IP is spent on a single sale.
questions.explanation: An offer is a one-time transaction, but IP is reused and sharpened with every delivery, so using it lowers cost, raises the ceiling on the work the practice can take, and makes it harder to copy.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to treat a compliance obligation as an inconvenient term the practice can accept as a calculated trade?
options: A compliance obligation is set from outside and binary, so the work is to meet it, not accept it as a risk.
A compliance obligation is a term that can be renegotiated with the client before signing.
A compliance obligation is a risk the practice carries only if the client agrees in writing.
A compliance obligation binds the model provider rather than the practice itself.
questions.explanation: Compliance is enforced from outside and is binary, so the only work is to build a control that meets the obligation rather than decide to accept it.

questions.question: What actually transfers delivery judgment from a principal to an operator?
options: Handing the operator the written standard to read until it is memorized.
Letting the operator shadow the principal for a full year before deciding.
Reviewing the operator's output against the acceptance criteria after each delivery.
A progression of observation, then committed decisions compared against the principal's, then earned autonomy, then independent judgment.
questions.explanation: Judgment transfers when the operator commits to a decision and sees the delta against the mentor's reasoning, not by being told the answer.

questions.question: Which three properties must a candidate service line pass before it is worth productizing?
options: Demand, competence, and repeatability.
Demand, margin, and headcount.
Competence, price, and duration.
Repeatability, brand, and geography.
questions.explanation: A line must have a market that will pay, be deliverable well without the principal's hands, and repeat across clients so shared method can be built and scaled.

questions.question: What is the hard requirement for a gate in a quality system?
options: That it happens at the point of delivery so nothing ships unreviewed.
That it is recorded in the quality system before the work advances.
That it has a named reviewer and a written checklist of criteria.
Separation: the author of the work does not pass their own work.
questions.explanation: A gate only works if the person who produced the work is not the one who passes it, since authors miss their own mistakes.

questions.question: When should a practice write down a reference architecture?
options: As soon as it decides to offer a class of work, so the first engagement can follow it.
After the second or third time it has done that kind of work, once the shape has repeated.
Only after a client asks for a formal methodology document.
Whenever a competitor publishes an equivalent pattern for the same problem.
questions.explanation: A pattern is only trustworthy once it has been earned by repetition, so a premature reference architecture is confident and wrong.

questions.question: Why does hourly pricing punish a practice that has captured IP?
options: Because clients compare hourly rates and always choose the cheapest.
Because capturing IP raises the cost of delivering each engagement.
Because cheaper delivery bills fewer hours, so greater efficiency yields a smaller bill.
Because hourly contracts forbid fixed-price add-ons to the catalog.
questions.explanation: Hourly revenue equals hours times rate, so every efficiency that cuts delivery time cuts the bill too, which turns the practice's biggest advantage into a reason to charge less.

questions.question: An account buys the lowest-margin work and drains senior capability from the practice. How should a principal treat it?
options: Renew it but staff it with junior operators to protect the margin.
Keep it, since all revenue is good and churn is always the enemy.
Convert it to an hourly model so the attention cost becomes visible.
Treat it as a candidate for intentional churn, freeing capability for accounts that compound.
questions.explanation: An account that consumes more capability than it returns is worth winding down deliberately, so the freed capability can fund accounts that compound.

questions.question: What is the key-person trap, and how is it remedied?
options: One consultant is the only one who can run a critical offer, and the remedy is cross-training so capability is held by the system.
The principal works too many hours, and the remedy is delegating the least important tasks.
A new hire ramps too slowly, and the remedy is a longer probation period.
The team depends on one client, and the remedy is signing more clients.
questions.explanation: If a capability lives in one person, the practice rents rather than owns it, so every sold capability needs more than one person who can run it, held by the method and the system instead.

questions.question: What property turns a written standard into a real one?
options: It is written in a comprehensive document the team agrees to follow.
A senior person enforces it by reviewing every deliverable by hand.
The executor runs it without deciding to, because the standard is loadable into the work.
It is published once at the start and never revised.
questions.explanation: A standard that lives in a document people must choose to obey is only a suggestion; it becomes real when it is encoded into the mechanism the work runs on, so following the method produces the standard output.

questions.question: Why does captured IP widen margin even when the price does not change?
options: Because it lowers the cost of delivery while the price stays set on the value of the outcome.
Because it lets the practice charge clients more for the same work.
Because it reduces the number of people needed to sell the work.
Because it allows utilization to run at 100 percent indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The price is anchored to the outcome, not the cost, so running delivery on captured method and tooling cuts cost per delivery and the difference becomes margin that funds the practice's future.

questions.question: Which three properties separate compounding internal tooling from a one-off expense?
options: It is fast, cheap, and fully automated.
It is documented, approved, and version controlled.
It is reused, improves with use, and has a named owner.
It is generic, portable, and independent of any single client.
questions.explanation: Tooling compounds only when it is reused, improves with each use, and has a named owner to keep it current.
